title: Silk cocoons sell near 12 piastres per oka in the 1840s
why: French demand later lifted the price to 45 piastres per oka by 1857, reshaping peasant incomes in the mountain.

title: Mountain sheikhs rebel against Bashir II and Egyptian rule
why: British-backed revolt by Druze and Maronite sheikhs opened the end of Ibrahim Pasha's nine-year occupation of Mount Lebanon.

title: Bashir II reports revolt crushed, exiles 57 rebel leaders to Egypt
why: Bashir handed Haydar Abu'l Lama and Fransis al-Khazen among others to the Egyptians, deepening grievances that fed the later Ottoman restoration.

title: Convention of London pledges allied action against Muhammad Ali in Syria
why: The Great Powers' treaty set the legal basis for ejecting Egypt from Syria and restoring Ottoman rule over Mount Lebanon.

title: British consul Richard Wood courts Maronite Patriarch with guarantees
why: Wood, charged by the Ottomans with Lebanese affairs, promised respect for Maronite Church privileges while Bashir II refused three offers to defect.

title: Sultan appoints Bashir Shihab III emir of Mount Lebanon
why: Ottoman choice to replace Bashir II; a weak emir whose tenure ended in 1841-42 and closed the Shihab emirate (other sources: firman of 8 Oct 1840).

title: Allied fleet bombards Beirut; British, Austrian and Ottoman force lands at Jounieh
why: Naval assault on Egyptian-held Beirut (other sources: 11 Sept); the landing at Jounieh armed local rebels against Ibrahim Pasha.

title: Allied forces hold Beirut, Sidon, Tyre and Haifa
why: Control of the coast cut Ibrahim Pasha's sea supply and collapsed Egyptian authority in Mount Lebanon within weeks.

title: Sultan's firman replaces Bashir II with Bashir Qasim
why: The decree addressed the 'Mountain of the Druzes', reflecting the pre-Egyptian balance that Maronite villagers contested.

title: Bashir II surrenders to the Ottomans and sails into exile in Malta
why: The long-ruling emir (since 1788) left with family and 113 retainers, later Istanbul; he died there in 1850.

title: Maronite villagers and Druze notables clash at Baqlin near Deir al-Qamar
why: A dispute over land and taxes after the Egyptian exit escalated into the first major Druze-Maronite fighting; over two dozen Druze reported killed.

title: Druze besiege emir Bashir Qasim in Deir al-Qamar for three weeks
why: Nakad shaykhs and others trapped the emir, then ambushed and beat him; hundreds of villagers across the Shuf died as war spread.

title: Restoration politics fuses religion and land rights in Shuf conflict
why: Historian Makdisi dates the age of political sectarianism in Mount Lebanon to this violence over Druze restitution versus Maronite equality claims.

title: Maronite Patriarch Hobeish refuses to cooperate with Omar Pasha
why: The Patriarch rejected any ruler not chosen by Lebanese, and the Pasha's petitions of support were exposed as bribed.

title: Sultan deposes Bashir III and appoints Omar Pasha governor
why: Ended Shihab rule; Omar Pasha, an Ottoman of Austrian birth, was rejected by Christians (other sources: deposition on 13 Dec 1842).

title: Sultan adopts partition of Mount Lebanon into Christian and Druze districts
why: The Double Qaimaqamate was born of European pressure; Beirut-Damascus road was the dividing line (other sources: 1 Dec 1843).

title: Bashir III summoned to Beirut and shipped to Constantinople
why: Closed the Shihab emirate for good; the Ottomans exploited the Druze siege of Deir al-Qamar (other sources date his removal to January 1842).

title: First qaimaqams named: Ahmad Arslan (Druze) and Haydar Abu'l Lama (Christian)
why: Each qaimaqam had a Druze and a Christian wakil handling justice and taxes for their own community, in a mixed southern district.

title: Portalis opens first mechanised silk factory at Btater, Matn
why: Start of industrial silk reeling in Mount Lebanon, which tied the mountain economy to Lyon and Marseille mills.

title: Amin Arslan succeeds Ahmad Arslan as Druze qaimaqam
why: He held the southern qaimaqamate until 1859, through the 1845 war and the peasant unrest before 1860.

title: Turkish governor installed in Deir al-Qamar after 1845 fighting
why: The Nakad lord Bashir Abu Nakad was driven from his seat there and later sought revenge, according to Jessup.

title: Ottoman special commissioner Shakib Efendi sent to Mount Lebanon
why: His 1845 règlement kept the two qaimaqamates; Ottoman sources list him among special commissioners sent to Mount Lebanon in 1845-46.

title: Amin Shihab, son of Bashir II, converts to Islam
why: Ended French hopes of restoring the Shihab emirate, per the HEMED course.

title: Said Jumblatt convenes Druze sheikhs at Mukhtara
why: Missionary Jessup records the grand meeting of Druze chiefs preceding the spring 1845 fighting.

title: Druze-Maronite war of 1845 erupts at Deir al-Qamar, Jezzine and Abeih
why: Second round of sectarian fighting under the Double Qaimaqamate (other sources: April 1845; ended early June).

title: Druze besiege Shihab emirs and Maronites in Abeih castle
why: American missionary William Thomson carried a flag of truce; British Colonel Rose's arrival saved hundreds of Christians, per Jessup. (corrected from 1845-05: Jessup dates the Abeih fighting to April; Lemans chronology gives late April to early June 1845)

title: Maronite version of Ten Articles of Peace signed in Beirut
why: Part of Shakib Efendi's reglement for the Double Qaimaqamate, imposed by Ottoman authorities on both communities.

title: Druze version of 1845 peace convention signed under Bahri Pasha
why: Companion text to the Maronite pledge, obliging both parties to end hostilities.

title: Tartibat of 22 June 1845 consolidate reorganised Kaimakamate regime
why: Arrangements issued by the Sidon governor after the 1845 war; Wajihi was suspected of stirring the strife and left in early 1846. (attribution corrected: source ties the 22 June 1845 tartibat to Shekib Efendi, not Wajihi Pasha)

title: Shakib Efendi proclaims amnesty and parity of treatment between the communities
why: Declared the quarrels forgiven by the sultan, treating Druze and Christians alike in the aftermath of the 1845 war.

title: Jesuit school opens at Ghazir
why: Missionary schools drove sectarian education in the mountain, in contrast to later secular projects like Bustani's National School.

title: Bashir II dies in exile in Istanbul
why: The emir who ruled from 1788 to 1840 is buried in the Armenian church in Galata.

title: Bashir Ahmad Abu'l Lama succeeds as Christian qaimaqam, curbs the Khazens
why: His moves against Khazen influence led the Khazens to stir peasants, a revolt that turned against the Khazens themselves.

title: Sultan's reform edict declares equality of all Ottoman subjects
why: Christian peasants cited the edict and the Tanzimat to challenge feudal privilege, Tanyus Shahin among them.

title: Bad weather and silk crisis halve Mount Lebanon silk output, 1856-58
why: The slump deepened peasant distress and fed the revolts that preceded 1860.

title: Silk is under a quarter of Beirut's 40 million franc exports
why: Before 1860 silk was important but not dominant; its share rose to 82.5 percent of exports by 1873.

title: Ottoman government grants Perthuis concession for Beirut-Damascus carriage road
why: Former French naval officer Edmond de Perthuis won an exclusive 50-year concession; fares were to be about 30 percent below existing rates.

title: Keserwan peasants lodge formal complaint against Khazens with Khurshid Pasha
why: First step of the peasant movement against Khazen feudal dues, led soon by Tanyus Shahin.

title: First telegraph link with Europe reported for Beirut
why: Traboulsi dates it 1858; other sources say Beirut's first line (to Damascus) came in 1861.

title: Khazens call Keserwan summit; peasants voice dissent instead
why: The sheikhs sought backing for a new qaimaqam but the gathering turned into a peasant protest.

title: Khalil al-Khuri publishes first issue of Hadiqat al-Akhbar
why: Beirut weekly, among the first private Arabic papers; semi-official from 1860 and closed in 1911.

title: Keserwan villages ally against the Khazen sheikhs
why: The alliance, a village-level pact, preceded Shahin's election as leader.

title: Road company issues first 200-franc call on shares
why: Circular 15 Nov 1858 opened the financial phase of Perthuis' concession.

title: Tanyus Shahin chosen wakil awwal of Keserwan peasants
why: A muleteer and blacksmith from Rayfoun became head of the first peasant uprising to oust a noble family in the mountain.

title: Shahin declares a republic in Keserwan with 100-member council
why: Government seated at Rayfoun from autumn, with about 1,000 militia and committees of village delegates.

title: Shahin leads 800 peasants to besiege Khazens at Ghosta
why: Armed revolt began; the Khazen sheikhs fled and their estates were plundered with little bloodshed.

title: Shia villagers of Byblos protest Keserwani raids
why: Shahin's men attacked Shia villages and demanded conversion, per Makdisi, hardening elite opposition while raising his popular standing.

title: Khazen sheikhs routed; 500-600 family members flee to Beirut
why: The peasant victory was unprecedented; a Khazen wife and daughter were killed at Ajaltoun in July.

title: Brawl at Beit Mery between Druze and Maronites leaves 20 dead
why: Followed by Bishop Tobia Aoun arming Maronite peasants; some sources date it 30 Aug and blame a children's quarrel.

title: Beirut population doubles as Christian refugees flood the city
why: Refugees from Matn, Shuf, Hasbaya and Zahle overwhelmed Beirut; Churchill counts 100,000 refugees in all.

title: Estimates of 1860 dead range from 7,000 to 25,000
why: Most sources say 7,000-11,000 in Mount Lebanon; Farley listed 326 villages and 560 churches destroyed.

title: Property losses put at four million pounds sterling
why: The war struck during the silk season, devastating the mountain's main cash crop.

title: Governor of Damascus Ahmed Pasha executed for negligence
why: Ottomans sacrificed him to appease European powers and prevent lasting occupation.

title: Britain sends Lord Dufferin to investigate the massacres
why: He joined the international tribunal alongside Fuad Pasha's court-martial, which sentenced Druze notables like Said Jumblatt.

title: Hadiqat al-Akhbar made semi-official at Fuad Pasha's request
why: Ottoman-backed status lasted until the official Suriya paper appeared.

title: Arabic Protestant New Testament (Smith-Van Dyck translation) first printed at Beirut; full Bible followed in 1865
why: Printed at the American Mission Press, with Bustani among translators. (title corrected: the 1860 printing was the New Testament; complete Bible printed 1865)

title: Maronite Bishop Tobia Aoun distributes arms in Mount Lebanon
why: His Beirut committee armed peasants before war; Patriarch's line urged calm, per Wikipedia summary of Fawaz.

title: Beirut-Damascus Road company calls up share capital in December 1860
why: Third call of 100 francs per share published in Le Moniteur, 23 Dec 1860, showing French investor money despite the war.
actors: Compagnie ottomane de la route de Beyrouth à Damas

title: Monastery at Aammiq looted and its father killed
why: First in a tit-for-tat chain of murders in mixed districts before the war.

title: Two Jezzine Christians murdered at Khan Iqlim al-Shumar
why: Next day four Christians were killed at Katuli, as roads in the mixed districts became unsafe.

title: Druze war council at Moukhtara appoints Said Jumblatt commander
why: Jumblatti and Yazbaki factions united under Jumblatt.

title: Maronites fire on Druze at entrance to Beirut
why: One killed, two wounded; the incident reignited fighting according to a Mutasarrifate summary.

title: Khurshid Pasha garrisons troops at Hazmiyeh
why: Christians read the deployment as a prelude to a Druze assault; European consuls supported it.

title: War begins as Shahin's militia advances to Baabda
why: The Keserwan force came for Naccache silk; Druze took it as provocation (British consul dated the war 29 May).

title: Druze and Maronites fight at Beit Mery and mixed Matn villages
why: Keserwani raids on Qarnayel, Btekhnay and Salima expelled Druze residents; houses burned both sides.

title: Clashes at Dahr al-Baidar open fighting near Zahle
why: A 200-strong Druze force met 400 Christians; Ali Imad was fatally wounded and died on 3 June.

title: Druze take Matn; 35-40 Maronite villages burned, about 600 killed
why: The Maronite force was routed at Beit Mery; some 60 villages near Beirut were destroyed over 29-31 May.

title: Harfush clan besieges Baalbek; 34 Bekaa Christian villages plundered
why: After Zahle's fall Sunni and Shia locals settled scores; Baalbek was largely destroyed.

title: 3,000-6,000 Christian refugees reach Damascus from Hasbaya and Rashaya
why: Mostly Greek Orthodox; aid came from churches and Muslim notables including Abd al-Qadir, raising local tension.

title: Deir al-Qamar surrenders to Druze after eight-hour assault
why: Plundered until 6 June, 130 houses destroyed; reported dead 70-100 Druze and 17-25 Christians.

title: Hasbaya falls; about 1,000 Christian males killed in government house
why: Emir Sa'ad al-Din Shihab and 16 other Shihab men also died; some 400 sheltered by Nayifa Jumblatt survived.

title: Christians of Dahr al-Ahmar flee to Rashaya as Druze burn villages
why: A dispute over arrests of Kfar Quq men set off violence in the southern Bekaa.

title: Rashaya stormed; Shihab emirs and men in government house killed
why: Hasbaya and Rashaya together cost roughly 1,800 Christian lives; Isma'il al-Atrash's Hauran Druze joined.

title: Zahle's militia attacks Qabb Ilyas and is repulsed
why: A second assault days later also failed, weakening the last major Christian stronghold.

title: Zahle falls to Druze and allies after surprise from the north
why: Khattar Imad disguised fighters as Christians; town emptied by 19 June; casualty estimates 40-900 Christians, 100-1,500 attackers.

title: Damascus celebrates the fall of Zahle
why: Muslim celebrations deepened tension; notables Mahmud Hamza and Ahmad Hasibi failed to stop them, per Fawaz.

title: Abd al-Qadir al-Jaza'iri begins defending Damascus Christian quarter
why: The exiled Algerian leader armed about 1,000 men, mostly Algerians, with French consul Lanusse's funds.

title: Deir al-Qamar massacre: 1,200 to 2,200 Christians killed
why: Disarmed Christians were slain in the government house; roughly 4,000 Ottoman troops did not intervene; town of 10,000 fell to about 400.

title: Khurshid Pasha reaches Deir al-Qamar after the killings
why: Missionary Jessup records the arrival after the massacre was over; Khurshid was later removed.

title: Beirut mobs demand execution of Christian suspect; acting governor complies
why: A Muslim man was killed 22-23 June; Ismail Pasha executed the suspect within 12 hours to avert riots, against consul wishes. (corrected from "22-23 June": source says the man was killed on 23 June)

title: Damascus governor places 14 cannons on the Citadel
why: Before the riots Ahmad Pasha installed guns as deterrence; consuls such as Brant doubted any danger (exact day not stated: early July).

title: Damascus riots begin after Muslim boys punished for desecrating crosses
why: Abd al-Karim al-Samman freed the boys and led crowds to the Christian quarter (other sources: 8 July start).

title: Mobs burn Bab Tuma and loot Damascus Christian homes and churches
why: Crowds estimated 20,000-50,000 of Muslims, Druze and Kurdish irregulars; Ottoman troops withdrew by midday.

title: Mob burns Russian, French, Dutch, Austrian and Belgian consulates in Damascus
why: Russian dragoman Khalil Shehadi was killed; only the British and Prussian consulates were spared.

title: Algerian Abd al-Qadir saves Christians during Damascus riots
why: His men rescued Lazarists, 150 children under Sisters of Charity and consuls; he later received European honours.

title: Spanish Franciscans and companions killed at Damascus convent
why: Franciscans ignored three offers of escort from Abd al-Qadir's men and were killed on the second day.

title: Violence in Damascus renewed on third day; hundreds seized from Muslim homes
why: Abd al-Qadir faced down a mob at his residence, where Christians sheltered, and protected French Lazarists and Sisters of Charity.

title: Fuad Pasha sails from Istanbul with troops to restore order
why: The foreign minister had full powers; his early action undercut the case for French intervention.

title: Killing in Damascus tapers off by 17 July
why: Violence slowed from 12 July; the Christian quarter was destroyed and most survivors fled to Beirut or Saidnaya.

title: Tanyus Shahin declares obedience to the sultan
why: Under pressure from Bishop Aoun, a de facto repudiation of the Keserwan revolt's legitimacy.

title: Fuad Pasha's tribunals execute Damascus rioters, 357 recorded
why: Ottoman and European sources record roughly 357 executions; a 22 August report gives 70 hanged in Damascus; earlier text says 110.

title: Maronite reprisal raids on Druze villages after French landing
why: Summary executions and burnings, smaller in scale than June but cementing demographic shifts in mixed districts.

title: Ottomans agree to up to 12,000 European troops for Syria
why: Protocol response to Damascus; France to supply half.

title: French expeditionary corps of 6,000 lands in Beirut
why: General Beaufort d'Hautpoul commanded it; the force stayed until June 1861, longer than the planned six months.

title: Convention of five powers and the Porte on intervention
why: Austria, Britain, France, Prussia and Russia formalised the Syria expeditionary framework.

title: Butrus al-Bustani issues first Nafir Suriyya broadside
why: Eleven bulletins ran to April 1861, urging unity under the idea of homeland (watan).

title: International commission meets in Beirut on the causes of 1860
why: Delegates blamed the 1842 partition; the work led to the Règlement Organique (another source: opened 5 September).

title: Youssef Karam named Christian qaimaqam by Fuad Pasha
why: Ehden-born leader governed the Christian areas until 1861 and resisted the Règlement.

title: Nayifa Jumblatt brought to Beirut and imprisoned
why: Hasbaya widows demanded the return of their menfolk, per Jessup; Fuad's court tried Druze leaders.

title: Beirut linked by telegraph to Damascus
why: Set up at Fuad Pasha's wish after 1860; Beirut-Istanbul followed in 1863.

title: Mutasarrifate seat at Deir al-Qamar under Governor Daud Pasha
why: Mount Lebanon separated from Syria; Ottoman Christian mutasarrif from Constantinople governed with a 12-member council.

title: Beirut population about 140,000 at start of 1860s
why: Damascus, a larger inland centre, had nearly 200,000; the road trip took about four days before 1863.

title: Youssef Karam defeats Shahin's forces between Rayfoun and Ashqout
why: Shahin fled; his republic effectively ended after reconciliation on 12 April.

title: Shahin reconciles with Karam under mediation of General Beaufort
why: Shahin submitted without conditions and later served as a judicial official in Rayfoun until his death in 1895.

title: Last Nafir Suriyya broadside published
why: Bustani turned to longer projects: National School, Al-Jinan and Muhit al-Muhit.

title: Draft Règlement for Mount Lebanon dated 1 May 1861
why: Draft became final settlement after mutual amendments; Article 1 set a Christian governor with Deir al-Qamar as seat.

title: Said Jumblatt dies in Beirut prison
why: Per Jessup he died in custody after the 1860 trials (May of 1861).

title: French expeditionary corps leaves Syria
why: The occupation lasted August 1860 to June 1861 despite British objections.

title: Règlement Organique and Beyoglu Protocol create Mutasarrifate; Daud Pasha appointed
why: Autonomous Mount Lebanon under a non-Lebanese Catholic governor, with a council of twelve; initially three years.

title: Mount Lebanon has 33 Lebanese-owned silk filatures
why: Grew to 101 by 1885 and 149 by 1893 as French mills bought mountain thread.

title: Matba'at al-Ma'arif press founded in Beirut by Khalil Sarkis
why: Part of the Beirut printing boom after Hadiqat al-Akhbar. (corrected from 1862: Arab Encyclopedia gives 1868, founded with the Bustani family)

title: Beirut-Damascus carriage road opens
why: Built by Perthuis' French-Ottoman company; trip fell from 3-4 days to about 13 hours.

title: Beirut linked by telegraph to Istanbul
why: Two years after the Damascus line.

title: Bustani opens al-Madrasa al-Wataniyya in Beirut
why: Secular, interconfessional National School with 115 boarders (other sources: 1862).

title: Règlement Organique revised and made permanent
why: Reconfirmed by the powers; Italy adhered in 1867.

title: Syrian Protestant College founded in Beirut
why: Daniel Bliss opened what became AUB, in the educational boom following 1860.

title: Youssef Karam leaves Lebanon for Algeria on French ship
why: He resisted the Mutasarrifate's non-native governor; exile ended his autonomy campaign.
